The court will hear a gerrymandering case Wednesday. Scott Bauer Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save MADISON — The Wisconsin Supreme Court will hear a gerrymandering case Wednesday that could decide if the maps for U.S. House seats should be redrawn in the state. Doug Poland, Law Forward director of litigation, and Jack Deschler of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School will make oral arguments before the seven-member, liberal-leaning court. Poland and Deschler discussed the case with media across the state in a Zoom conference call. “It’s a question that is simple, but has enormous consequences for Wisconsin voters,” Poland said. “Our case is about a different kind of gerrymander. They are designed to lock in safe seats.” Wisconsin has eight U.S. House seats. Currently, Republicans hold six of the eight seats. However, Poland points out that no incumbent in Wisconsin has lost a race in the past decade, so he contends the maps are unfair because they essentially allow the congressmen to choose their voters. He said they will argue this is an “anti-competitive gerrymandering case.” The current maps “pre-ordain the elections, rather than require the candidates to run on the issues,” Poland contends. “The maps are engineered to lock in a result before Election Day.” Poland said their argument isn’t about Republican-set maps, but rather about maps that protect all incumbents. “We do not think it is true the lawsuit targets national districts,” he said. “Our challenge is based solely on Wisconsin state law.” Deschler was asked about the national implications for this case. “This is part of a national movement,” Deschler said. “We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will be the next step in this movement. “We’re asking for the Supreme Court to say any anti-competitive gerrymander is not allowed.” Deschler added: “We think the Wisconsin Constitution provides for this.” Poland said there is a trial date set for spring 2027 before a trial court. Any appeal would go back to the state Supreme Court. “We do think this could be resolved rather quickly,” Poland said. “We think it can be wrapped up in six or seven months.” Poland stressed that the court is not being asked to decide on the maps in this argument. “All we’re asking is the Supreme Court recognize our claim is a valid claim under state law,” Poland said. “We’re not asking the Supreme Court to do anything more than recognize our claim at this point.” He added: “We do think the court does have the authority to rule on our claim.” Deschler said the maps do not benefit one party or the other, but instead, they argue it makes all eight seats safe for the incumbents. “It’s one of the reasons we think the circuit court is fit to rule on this,” Deschler said. Poland provided a timeline for how maps could be redrawn if he wins his case. “We’d like to urge the court to rule on this very quickly, certainly by the end of the year,” Poland said. “We want to make sure we have final district in place by about April of 2028.” Deschler said that if the court agrees with them, it’s his hope that other states look at it. “We’re hoping the Wisconsin Supreme Court sets an example for other states to follow,” Deschler said. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/merz-accu.text: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Updated Tue, November 10, 2026 at 4:48 PM UTC 0 Friedrich Merz (left) welcoming the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in Berlin in early November.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine, triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month. The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort. “What the chancellor is doing is typical blackmail, and I will not give in to it,” Slovakia’s Russia-friendly prime minister , Robert Fico, told reporters in Bratislava. He was speaking alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš, whose populist government also rejects taking part in a future loan for Ukraine. “I do not know why he is saying it,” Babiš said, referring to Merz’s position. Merz wants EU leaders to discuss Ukraine’s financing needs at a summit in Dublin on Friday. “We must continue to support Ukraine in its fight to defend itself. This is in our shared vital interest,” he wrote in a letter, seen by the Guardian, to the European Council president, António Costa, who will chair the meeting. “And yet, bilateral assistance to Ukraine is distributed unevenly and carried mostly by only a few member states.” The EU last year agreed to lend Ukraine €90bn , which was intended to cover two-thirds of its military and civilian costs for 2026 and 2027. But since then, Russia’s relentless bombardment has heaped more costs on Kyiv, prompting President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to call for €70bn to fill a budget shortfall . The EU has endorsed Zelenskyy’s figures and pledged to find €45bn, with Ukraine’s other allies, such as the UK and Canada, expected to provide the rest. Merz last year led an effort to use Russia’s €210bn sovereign wealth frozen in the EU, but the plan was scuppered by opposition led by Belgium, which hosts most of the funds at Brussels. The €90bn loan was the fallback plan. Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia, which opted out of that loan, have indicated they will stay out of the next round. Those three member states have now been joined by Bulgaria, following the election of Moscow-friendly prime minister Rumen Radev last April. The issue of Ukraine’s financing is now ricocheting into tortuous negotiations on the EU budget for 2028-34. Germany, the largest net contributor, wants steep cuts in the proposed budget, while opposing generous EU funding for member states that refuse to chip in to Ukraine’s financial needs. In his letter Merz writes that “a collective commitment … without exception” is an “essential pre-requisite” for resolving Ukraine’s funding shortfall and “discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications”. He also states that all member states need to contribute to a “sound” financial perspective for Ukraine from 2028 in the context of the EU’s next seven-year budget, known as the multiannual financial framework. A German government official said: “Financial support for Ukraine of all EU member states is essential in order to successfully complete the MFF.” Berlin is also seeking to switch the decision-making process on funding Ukraine to a qualified-majority vote, rather than unanimity, in order to prevent one government from blocking EU decisions. The letter reflects growing exasperation from the EU’s northern member states that are Ukraine’s most generous backers over smaller contributions from other EU member states in central and southern Europe. The task of finding an agreement on the budget falls to Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister. He wants a deal by the end of the year, before elections in France, Poland and Italy in 2027 that are likely to complicate the task. A spokesperson for Costa confirmed receipt of the letter without commenting on details. “President Costa will make time for interventions on Ukraine at the informal European Council in Dublin this week,” the spokesperson said, adding that Ukraine finance would be discussed at a special summit dedicated to the EU budget on 26-27 November.
